title: The Day Before the Foreclosure Referral: What a Default Desk Has to Prove, and Prove Again on the Day Counsel Files
summary: A foreclosure referral sent a week early, or while a complete loss mitigation application sat unreviewed, is the kind of Regulation X violation that shows up in a borrower's lawsuit before it shows up in an exam. The checks behind the 120-day rule in 12 CFR 1024.41(f), the dual-tracking limits in 1024.41(g), the SCRA and bankruptcy holds, and state pre-foreclosure notices, and why we re-run every one of them on the day the first notice is filed, not only the day the file is referred.
body_markdown:
## Who This Is For


Heads of Servicing, default and foreclosure managers, and servicing compliance officers at banks, credit unions and independent mortgage banks. Also the MSR owner whose subservicer makes these referrals in the owner's name.


## The Referral Is the Point of No Return


A lot happens to a delinquent mortgage before foreclosure, and most of it can be corrected. A late acknowledgment letter can be followed by a correct one. A miscalculated escrow shortage can be refunded. The first notice or filing for foreclosure is different. Once a complaint is filed or a notice of default is recorded, it is a public record, it carries legal fees that land on the borrower's account, and if it was premature, the borrower has a claim.[Regulation X at 12 CFR 1024.41](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1024/41/) is one of the few servicing provisions with a private right of action, which RESPA section 6(f) supplies, so a premature or dual-tracked referral tends to be found by the borrower's attorney rather than the servicer's QC.


That is why referral review exists as a step at most servicers. Someone pulls the file, confirms the loan is eligible for referral, and signs off before it goes to counsel. The problem is that review happens on one day, and counsel files on a later one, and the rules apply on the day of filing.


## Gate One: More Than 120 Days Delinquent


Under 1024.41(f)(1), a servicer may not make the first notice or filing required by state law for any judicial or non-judicial foreclosure unless the borrower's mortgage loan obligation is more than 120 days delinquent, the foreclosure is based on a due-on-sale violation, or the servicer is joining a subordinate lienholder's foreclosure. Small servicers are bound by this one too, under 1024.41(j).


Counting the 120 days used to be a source of argument. The CFPB settled most of it in the 2016 servicing amendments by defining delinquency in[12 CFR 1024.31](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1024/31/) : a borrower is delinquent beginning on the date a periodic payment sufficient to cover principal, interest and, if applicable, escrow becomes due and unpaid, until no periodic payment is due and unpaid. The commentary allows a servicer to credit a payment to the oldest outstanding periodic payment. So the count runs from the oldest unpaid installment, and every payment the borrower made since then can move it.


This is where referral review goes wrong in practice. A borrower who sent two partial payments that sat in suspense has a different delinquency date depending on whether and when the suspense balance reached a full periodic payment and was applied. If the servicing system's delinquency date was set before those payments, the count is wrong. Our post on[partial payments and suspense accounts](https://www.seiright.com/blog/mortgage-payment-application-partial-payments-suspense-ai-servicing-reg-z-prompt-crediting) covers how that happens. The[Default Management Desk](https://www.seiright.com/for-servicers/default-management-desk) does not take the system's days-delinquent field on trust. It recomputes the delinquency date from the payment history, applying each payment and suspense movement in order, and if its date disagrees with the system's, the referral stops until a person reconciles the two.


The "first notice or filing" also depends on the state. The official commentary ties it to the foreclosure procedure under applicable state law, which in practice means the first document that has to be filed with a court, recorded or published to start the foreclosure. In a judicial state that is usually the complaint. In a non-judicial state it may be a recorded notice of default. The desk carries that definition per state in the[Rulebook](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#rulebook) , so the 120-day test is run against the date that document will actually be filed or recorded, which is the date counsel gives back, not the referral date.


## Gate Two: No Complete Application Pending


Dual tracking is the practice of moving a foreclosure forward while the borrower is being evaluated for a workout. Regulation X restricts it in two places.


Under 1024.41(f)(2), if a borrower submits a complete loss mitigation application during the pre-foreclosure review period, or before the first notice or filing, the servicer may not make the first notice or filing unless it has sent the borrower a notice that they are not eligible for any option and any appeal is over, the borrower has rejected every option offered, or the borrower has failed to perform under an agreement. Under 1024.41(g), if a complete application arrives after the first filing but more than 37 days before a scheduled sale, the servicer may not move for judgment or an order of sale, or conduct the sale, until one of the same three conditions is met.


Two details make this harder than it reads. The first is that "complete" includes applications Regulation X treats as complete. Under 1024.41(c)(2)(iv), when a servicer has received all the documents it asked for but then needs something else to evaluate the application, the application is treated as complete for purposes of (f)(2) and (g) until the borrower has had a reasonable chance to supply it. A file the loss mitigation team considers incomplete may be complete for dual-tracking purposes. The second is that applications arrive through every channel: a fax, an upload, a package handed to a housing counselor, an email to the single point of contact. A package received by the mailroom on Tuesday and indexed on Thursday was received on Tuesday.


So gate two is a query across everything the servicer has received, not a look at the loss mitigation system's status field. The[Indexing Manager](https://www.seiright.com/for-servicers/indexing-manager) files every incoming document the day it lands with its received date, and the[Loss Mitigation Agent](https://www.seiright.com/for-servicers/loss-mitigation-agent) tracks each application's completeness state, including the "treated as complete" state. The referral gate reads both. Our post on the[Regulation X loss mitigation clock](https://www.seiright.com/blog/ai-agents-mortgage-loss-mitigation-regulation-x-servicer-playbook) covers the evaluation side.


## Gate Three: Holds That Override the Clock


Some borrowers cannot be referred even when they are more than 120 days delinquent with no application pending.


The Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, at[50 U.S.C. 3953](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/50/3953) , voids a foreclosure sale, without a court order, of a servicemember's property on a mortgage that originated before military service, during service and for one year after it ends. That requires a current check of the Defense Manpower Data Center, not the result from onboarding. Our post on[SCRA compliance](https://www.seiright.com/blog/scra-compliance-ai-agents-servicemembers-dmdc) covers the DMDC process. A bankruptcy filing triggers the automatic stay under[11 U.S.C. 362](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/11/362) , and our post on[bankruptcy servicing](https://www.seiright.com/blog/bankruptcy-mortgage-servicing-ai-agents-chapter-7-13-automatic-stay) covers how the stay and the bankruptcy periodic statement rules interact. A pending notice of error that asserts a servicing mistake can also matter, because 1024.35 limits adverse credit reporting while the error is investigated, and an unresolved error on the payment history is often the same error that makes the delinquency count wrong.


Investor and insurer rules add their own. FHA, for example, requires the servicer to start foreclosure or acquire the property by other means within six months of default under[24 CFR 203.355](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-24/subtitle-B/chapter-II/subchapter-B/part-203/subpart-B/section-203.355) , unless an exception applies, and missing that deadline costs interest on the claim, which our post on[FHA claim curtailment](https://www.seiright.com/blog/fha-mortgage-insurance-claim-preparation-curtailment-ai-default-servicing-24-cfr-203-402) works through. So the referral date has a floor from Regulation X and, on many loans, a ceiling from the investor.


## Gate Four: The State's Own Notices


Many states require their own notice before foreclosure can begin. New York's[RPAPL 1304](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/RPA/1304) requires a notice at least 90 days before commencing a foreclosure action on a home loan, sent by registered or certified mail and first-class mail, with a list of housing counseling agencies, and New York courts have dismissed foreclosure actions where the servicer could not prove the notice was mailed correctly. California's[Civil Code 2923.5](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2923.5) requires the servicer to contact the borrower, or make diligent efforts to, at least 30 days before recording a notice of default. Each state's requirement is a rule with its own trigger, wait and proof standard, and the proof is usually the mailing record, not the letter.


The desk checks that each required notice for the property's state exists, was sent by the required method, and has a wait period that ends before the expected filing date. Where the proof is a certified mail receipt, it checks that the receipt is in the file.


## Why We Run the Gates Twice


When we set up the referral workflow, the instinct was to run all four gates at referral and attach the result to the package. We changed that because the referral date and the filing date can be weeks apart, and every gate can change in between. A complete application can arrive. A borrower can be called to active duty. A bankruptcy can be filed. A payment can post and reset the delinquency count.


So the[Orchestrator](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works) holds the referral as a goal that is not finished when the package goes to counsel. It re-runs every gate when counsel returns the expected filing date, and again on the day before filing. If any gate fails, the desk sends counsel a hold with the reason and the evidence, and puts the file in front of the default team. The desk does not refer a loan to foreclosure and does not tell counsel to proceed. A person on the default team makes that call, with each gate's result, the date it was checked and the document behind it in the[Evidence Trail](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#evidence-trail) .


That record is also the defense. When a borrower's attorney claims the first filing was premature, the servicer's answer is a dated chain: the delinquency date and the payments that set it, the loss mitigation status on the day of filing, the DMDC result, the state notice and its mailing receipt. Sei AI keeps that chain on the loan because building it after a complaint arrives is how servicers discover they cannot.


The 120-day rule has been in force since 2014. What still goes wrong is timing, because the review and the filing happen on different days and the file changes between them.
